questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Recognizing professional limits and obtaining qualified assistance
questions.performanceIndicator: Provide competent service when an assignment exceeds current expertise
questions.scenarioContext: A security manager is asked to lead a specialized investigation involving techniques the manager has never practiced. Executives expect an immediate conclusion and do not realize that the manager lacks the required expertise.
questions.prompt: What is the manager's BEST course of action?

choices.A: Accept the assignment silently and learn the techniques while handling the evidence
choices.B: Disclose the limitation and obtain appropriately qualified assistance while preserving responsibility and confidentiality
choices.C: Decline all involvement and publicly explain why management selected the wrong person
choices.D: Issue a preliminary conclusion based only on experience from unrelated investigations

questions.explanation: Professional competence requires an honest disclosure of relevant limitations and the use of qualified assistance when necessary. The manager can remain accountable while ensuring that specialized work is performed properly. Learning on live evidence risks error, public criticism may breach confidentiality, and an unsupported conclusion would mislead decision-makers.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Identifying a confidentiality breach in business communications
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply the CIA triad when accurate information reaches an unauthorized recipient
questions.scenarioContext: An employee sends an accurate compensation report to an external recipient who has no authorization to view it. The report remains available to authorized staff and is not modified.
questions.prompt: Which security objective has been MOST directly compromised?

choices.A: Availability
choices.B: Authenticity
choices.C: Integrity
choices.D: Confidentiality

questions.explanation: Confidentiality limits information disclosure to authorized parties, so delivery to an unauthorized recipient is a direct violation. The report remained accurate and accessible, leaving integrity and availability intact. Authenticity addresses whether an identity or item is genuine rather than whether the recipient was permitted to see the content.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Using risk appetite to guide strategic security decisions
questions.performanceIndicator: Connect executive risk direction to investment and escalation priorities
questions.scenarioContext: A media enterprise has approved a very low appetite for interruptions to its live broadcasting service but a moderate appetite for delays in an internal archival process. Both areas request the same limited resilience funding.
questions.prompt: How should the governance committee use this information?

choices.A: Prioritize treatments according to business impact and the approved appetite for each service
choices.B: Divide funding equally because governance should not distinguish between business objectives
choices.C: Let technical teams redefine risk appetite after selecting their preferred solutions
choices.D: Fund the archival process first because it accepts more risk

questions.explanation: Risk appetite expresses executive direction about the types and amounts of risk the organization is willing to pursue or retain. Combined with business impact, it should guide treatment priority and escalation. Equal allocation may ignore strategic needs, technical teams should not redefine executive appetite, and greater willingness to accept archival delay does not justify prioritizing it over the low-appetite service.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Separating governance oversight from control operation
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify complementary responsibilities that support accountability and independent challenge
questions.prompt: Which 2 arrangements BEST support sound security governance? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Business leaders own material risk decisions within delegated authority
choices.B: Control operators approve their own unresolved exceptions without oversight
choices.C: The security team accepts every enterprise risk because it provides technical advice
choices.D: An oversight function can challenge risk decisions and report significant issues through an appropriate channel
choices.E: System administrators define organizational risk appetite independently

questions.explanation: Accountable business leaders should own material risk decisions, while an oversight function provides independent challenge and escalation. Control operators approving their own exceptions weakens objectivity. Security advisers do not automatically own business risk, and system administrators do not set enterprise risk appetite without delegated governance authority.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Integrating security into a business transformation program
questions.performanceIndicator: Embed governance requirements before strategic design choices become fixed
questions.scenarioContext: A national retailer begins a major transformation that will change customer services, operating processes, partners, and data flows. Security is scheduled to review the program only after contracts and designs are finalized.
questions.prompt: What should the CISO recommend?

choices.A: Delay security involvement until implementation reveals which risks actually occur
choices.B: Let each supplier determine the retailer's acceptable business risk
choices.C: Include security, privacy, legal, and risk stakeholders in governance and design decisions from the outset
choices.D: Require one identical technical control for every process before analyzing business needs

questions.explanation: Early integration lets the program identify obligations, dependencies, risk ownership, and treatment needs while strategic choices can still be changed. Waiting creates costly late-stage findings, suppliers cannot set the retailer's appetite, and a uniform control imposed before analysis may not address differing risks or objectives.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Escalating a governance decision that exceeds delegated authority
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply documented decision rights to a strategic security exception
questions.scenarioContext: A regional manager wants to approve an exception whose potential impact exceeds the manager's documented authority. The exception supports an important launch, and delaying the decision could affect revenue.
questions.prompt: What should the security adviser recommend NEXT?

choices.A: Allow the manager to approve it because revenue impact expands delegated authority
choices.B: Escalate the documented risk and business rationale to the authorized decision-maker
choices.C: Approve the exception on behalf of the manager to keep the launch on schedule
choices.D: Remove the impact estimate so the request fits the manager's authority

questions.explanation: Decision rights remain governed by delegated authority even when a business deadline is important. The adviser should provide the authorized owner with the risk, rationale, options, and urgency needed for an informed decision. Neither commercial pressure nor altered documentation gives the manager or adviser additional acceptance authority.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Classifying an investigation required by an industry agreement
questions.performanceIndicator: Distinguish contractual industry review from government and internal proceedings
questions.scenarioContext: After a suspected payment-data incident, a merchant's agreement requires an independent investigation under an industry security program. No prosecutor or regulator has initiated the review.
questions.prompt: What type of investigation is MOST directly described?

choices.A: An industry-standards or contractual investigation
choices.B: A criminal prosecution
choices.C: An administrative licensing hearing
choices.D: A civil lawsuit for damages

questions.explanation: The investigation arises from an industry program and contractual agreement, so its scope and evidence requirements are primarily driven by those obligations. A criminal prosecution requires government action, an administrative hearing involves a regulatory authority, and a civil lawsuit is a judicial dispute between parties.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Maintaining the currency and authority of security policies
questions.performanceIndicator: Trigger governed review when organizational and legal assumptions change
questions.scenarioContext: A transportation company has not reviewed its information security policy for six years. Since approval, the company has entered new jurisdictions, acquired two businesses, and changed its operating model.
questions.prompt: Which action is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Keep the policy unchanged because its original approval remains permanent
choices.B: Let system administrators rewrite and approve the policy without business input
choices.C: Perform a governed review, update affected requirements, obtain authorized approval, and communicate the changes
choices.D: Replace the policy with informal guidance that each business unit may interpret independently

questions.explanation: Material changes in law, structure, and operations can invalidate policy assumptions. A controlled lifecycle includes review, stakeholder input, revision, authorized approval, communication, and later maintenance. Original approval is not permanent, technical personnel alone should not set enterprise direction, and informal guidance cannot replace a mandatory policy.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Assessing a new purpose for previously collected personal data
questions.performanceIndicator: Evaluate legal basis, notice, compatibility, and proportionality before secondary use
questions.scenarioContext: A delivery company collected location data to route drivers safely. Marketing now wants to use the historical data to build individual lifestyle profiles, a purpose not described when the information was collected.
questions.prompt: What should privacy leadership require BEFORE approving the new use?

choices.A: Approval by marketing alone because the organization already possesses the data
choices.B: Immediate profiling before retention periods remove older records
choices.C: A technical copy of the data stored under a different filename
choices.D: Assessment of purpose compatibility, legal basis, transparency, necessity, retention, and individual rights

questions.explanation: Possessing personal data does not automatically authorize every later use. The organization should assess whether the new purpose is compatible and lawful, whether people need additional information or choices, and whether the processing is necessary and proportionate. Marketing approval, urgency, or copying the data does not resolve those obligations.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Preserving trade secret protection through reasonable measures
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify complementary contractual and access-governance safeguards
questions.scenarioContext: A specialty manufacturer relies on a confidential formula that derives value from not being generally known. The company wants to strengthen the legal and organizational basis for treating it as a trade secret.
questions.prompt: Which 2 actions are MOST appropriate? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Publish the formula while labeling it confidential
choices.B: Restrict access according to business need and maintain evidence of authorized handling
choices.C: Avoid identifying the information internally so employees are not alerted to its value
choices.D: File the formula as a trademark without controlling disclosure
choices.E: Use suitable confidentiality agreements and communicate continuing duties to authorized recipients

questions.explanation: Trade secret protection depends on secrecy and reasonable measures to preserve it. Need-based access, accountable handling, confidentiality agreements, and clear duties support that objective. Public disclosure destroys secrecy, failing to identify sensitive information weakens protection, and trademark registration does not protect a confidential formula from disclosure.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Evaluating import restrictions before acquiring controlled technology
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate legal classification and authorization before cross-border acquisition
questions.scenarioContext: A research institute plans to acquire specialized security equipment from another country. Procurement assumes that only the seller must consider cross-border controls and that the buyer has no import responsibilities.
questions.prompt: What should the institute determine before completing the purchase?

choices.A: Whether only the equipment's color affects import eligibility
choices.B: Whether classification, destination, end use, recipient, customs, licensing, or other import requirements apply
choices.C: Whether the seller is willing to omit the equipment description from shipping records
choices.D: Whether internal approval can replace government authorization

questions.explanation: The importing organization must identify the classification, end use, parties, customs rules, licenses, and other authorizations that apply in relevant jurisdictions. A seller's duties do not eliminate the buyer's obligations. Incomplete shipping records or internal approval cannot substitute for accurate declarations and required government authorization.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Separating factual investigation from legal conclusions
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate technical findings with qualified legal interpretation
questions.scenarioContext: An incident investigator confirms that protected records were accessed by an unauthorized account. The facts may trigger several contractual and statutory duties, but the investigator has no authority to interpret the governing law.
questions.prompt: What should the investigator do NEXT?

choices.A: Preserve and report the verified facts, then coordinate with authorized legal and business stakeholders on applicable duties
choices.B: Declare that every possible law was violated and notify all jurisdictions immediately
choices.C: Withhold the findings until the investigator can independently provide a legal opinion
choices.D: Delete evidence that does not support the first suspected legal theory

questions.explanation: The investigator should establish and preserve reliable facts within the assigned role, while qualified and authorized stakeholders determine legal and contractual consequences. Broad unsupported conclusions can produce inaccurate action, waiting for personal legal expertise delays response, and deleting contrary evidence compromises integrity and defensibility.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Calculating annualized loss expectancy from asset value, exposure factor, and event frequency
questions.performanceIndicator: Perform a complete quantitative risk calculation using self-contained values
questions.prompt: An illustrative asset is valued at $500,000. A loss event would create a 40 percent exposure, and the event is expected once every four years. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
questions.explanation: The single loss expectancy is $500,000 × 0.40, or $200,000. One event every four years gives an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.25. Multiplying $200,000 by 0.25 produces an annualized loss expectancy of $50,000. The other values omit or misapply one of the inputs.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Recognizing risk mitigation through reduced likelihood
questions.performanceIndicator: Classify a treatment that lowers exposure while the business activity continues
questions.scenarioContext: A wholesaler continues offering an online service but adds governance and preventive safeguards that materially reduce the likelihood of a defined loss scenario. The organization retains the remaining exposure.
questions.prompt: Which risk treatment strategy is being used?

choices.A: Acceptance without treatment
choices.B: Avoidance
choices.C: Transfer
choices.D: Mitigation

questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk while the underlying activity continues. Avoidance would discontinue the activity, transfer would allocate specified consequences to another party, and untreated acceptance would retain the exposure without the additional safeguards described.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Distinguishing inherent risk from residual risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Interpret exposure before and after the effect of controls
questions.scenarioContext: A healthcare billing process has a high level of exposure before safeguards are considered. After preventive and detective controls are applied, the remaining exposure is rated moderate.
questions.prompt: What does the moderate rating represent?

choices.A: Transferred risk owned entirely by a third party
choices.B: Residual risk remaining after controls are considered
choices.C: Inherent risk before safeguards are evaluated
choices.D: Risk appetite approved for every business process

questions.explanation: Residual risk is the exposure that remains after the effects of controls and other treatments are considered. The high pre-control rating is inherent risk. A residual rating does not show that risk was transferred, nor is it the same as the organization's broader risk appetite.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Establishing a sound threat-modeling foundation
questions.performanceIndicator: Define scope and systematically enumerate threats before prioritizing treatments
questions.prompt: Which 2 activities should occur as foundational parts of a structured threat-modeling exercise? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Define the system scope, assets, data flows, entry points, and trust boundaries
choices.B: Purchase a security product before identifying the threats it should address
choices.C: Enumerate and analyze threats using a consistent methodology, then prioritize them by risk
choices.D: Assume the design is safe when no prior incident has been reported
choices.E: Exclude business stakeholders because threat modeling is only a coding activity

questions.explanation: Threat modeling begins with an accurate understanding of scope, assets, flows, entry points, and trust boundaries. A consistent methodology then helps identify and prioritize relevant threats. Selecting products first reverses the analysis, absence of known incidents is not evidence of safety, and business context is needed to evaluate impact and priorities.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Responding to a material change in a critical vendor's risk profile
questions.performanceIndicator: Reassess treatment and contractual rights when ongoing monitoring reveals change
questions.scenarioContext: Ongoing monitoring shows that a critical records provider has changed ownership, replaced key subcontractors, and suffered repeated service failures. The provider passed due diligence three years ago.
questions.prompt: What should the vendor risk owner do FIRST?

choices.A: Perform a risk-based reassessment and evaluate treatment, escalation, and contractual options
choices.B: Rely on the original review because completed due diligence remains valid for the contract term
choices.C: Ignore ownership and subcontractor changes unless a confirmed data loss occurs
choices.D: Renew the agreement early to demonstrate confidence in the provider

questions.explanation: Material changes and repeated failures can invalidate prior assumptions, so the organization should reassess current exposure and use available treatment and contractual mechanisms. Due diligence is ongoing rather than permanent. Waiting for confirmed loss is reactive, and early renewal would reduce leverage before the changed risk is understood.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Tiering minimum supplier security requirements by risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Match due-diligence depth and contract controls to data, access, and criticality
questions.scenarioContext: A university applies the same lengthy security questionnaire and contract schedule to a catering supplier with no system access and to a provider that hosts sensitive research data. Reviews are slow, and high-risk relationships receive no additional scrutiny.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would be MOST effective?

choices.A: Eliminate supplier reviews so procurement can focus on delivery performance
choices.B: Use price as the only factor for determining security requirements
choices.C: Create risk tiers based on access, data sensitivity, criticality, and dependency, with requirements matched to each tier
choices.D: Apply the low-risk supplier requirements to every relationship for consistency

questions.explanation: Risk tiering directs assessment effort and contractual safeguards toward relationships with greater access, sensitive data, criticality, or dependency. It also avoids unnecessary burden on low-risk suppliers. Eliminating reviews, using price alone, or applying the weakest requirements universally would leave material supply-chain exposure insufficiently governed.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Using maximum tolerable downtime to constrain recovery planning
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize the disruption limit beyond which business harm becomes unacceptable
questions.scenarioContext: A business impact analysis finds that a laboratory reporting process can be interrupted for no more than ten hours before consequences become unacceptable. The proposed recovery strategy is expected to restore the process in fourteen hours.
questions.prompt: What should the continuity manager conclude?

choices.A: The strategy is acceptable because recovery objectives are optional estimates
choices.B: The fourteen-hour estimate is a recovery point objective for data loss
choices.C: The process should be removed from the continuity plan
choices.D: The strategy does not meet the maximum tolerable downtime and requires revision or additional capability

questions.explanation: Maximum tolerable downtime is the disruption limit beyond which the business impact becomes unacceptable. A strategy expected to recover after that limit does not meet the requirement and must be revised. The value concerns outage duration rather than data loss, and removing the process from the plan would hide rather than resolve the gap.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Reviewing access and obligations after an internal role transfer
questions.performanceIndicator: Treat job changes as controlled personnel-security events
questions.scenarioContext: An employee transfers from payroll administration to facilities planning. The employee receives new access but retains all payroll privileges because the account was not included in the transfer workflow.
questions.prompt: What control improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Retain all prior access in case the former team needs occasional assistance
choices.B: Trigger a role-change process that reviews old and new access, conflicts, agreements, training, and ownership approvals
choices.C: Create a second identity so old privileges remain available but less visible
choices.D: Let the employee decide which payroll privileges are still necessary

questions.explanation: Internal transfers require controlled review just as onboarding and departure do. Prior access should be removed unless a current, approved need exists, and new responsibilities may require updated training or agreements. Retained or hidden privileges create accumulation risk, and employees should not approve their own access.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Managing security obligations when a consultant engagement ends
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate access revocation, asset return, data disposition, and continuing duties
questions.scenarioContext: A consultant completes an engagement involving confidential design material. The project manager confirms that deliverables are accepted, but no one has addressed access, borrowed equipment, local copies, or continuing confidentiality duties.
questions.prompt: Which action should occur NEXT?

choices.A: Execute the documented offboarding process, including access removal, asset return, authorized data disposition, and confirmation of surviving obligations
choices.B: Keep access active for convenience in case another project begins later
choices.C: Allow the consultant to retain every local copy as a professional portfolio
choices.D: Delete all organizational records of the engagement after deliverable acceptance

questions.explanation: Contractor offboarding should promptly remove access, recover assets, govern copies and records, and reinforce obligations that continue after the engagement. Convenience does not justify dormant access, portfolio use requires explicit authorization, and deleting organizational records may violate business, evidentiary, or retention needs.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Reinforcing secure behavior after an awareness assessment
questions.performanceIndicator: Combine targeted learning with a safe reporting mechanism
questions.prompt: An awareness assessment shows that employees recognize suspicious messages but hesitate to report them because they fear punishment for mistakes. Which 2 program actions would BEST address the finding? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Stop measuring reporting behavior so poor results are not visible
choices.B: Provide targeted practice that includes the exact reporting process and expected response
choices.C: Publish the names of employees who made reporting errors
choices.D: Promote a clear, accessible, and supportive reporting channel with appropriate feedback
choices.E: Replace awareness activities with a statement that employees are solely responsible for every incident

questions.explanation: Targeted practice builds the specific reporting skill, while an accessible and supportive channel reduces hesitation and reinforces desired behavior. Hiding results prevents improvement, public blame discourages reporting, and assigning total incident responsibility to employees ignores organizational processes and controls.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Selecting a continuity strategy from business impact requirements
questions.performanceIndicator: Compare feasible recovery options against time, capability, and cost constraints
questions.scenarioContext: A financial cooperative has completed its business impact analysis and identified required recovery timeframes, minimum staffing, external dependencies, and acceptable manual workarounds. Several continuity strategies differ greatly in cost and capability.
questions.prompt: How should leadership select the strategy?

choices.A: Choose the most expensive option because cost proves resilience
choices.B: Let the technology team select based only on preferred tools
choices.C: Compare each option with BIA requirements, risk appetite, dependencies, feasibility, and total cost
choices.D: Choose the slowest option because longer recovery creates more planning time

questions.explanation: Continuity strategy selection should trace to the BIA and balance required capability, dependencies, feasibility, risk direction, and total cost. Price alone does not prove suitability, technology preference ignores broader business needs, and a slower option may fail the established recovery requirements.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Designing reliable crisis communications for a major disruption
questions.performanceIndicator: Establish authorized messages, alternate channels, stakeholder mapping, and validation
questions.scenarioContext: During a prolonged outage, different managers send conflicting updates to employees, customers, regulators, and suppliers. The normal email service is unavailable, and no one knows who may approve public statements.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would BEST address the continuity weakness?

choices.A: Allow every manager to publish independent estimates so communication remains fast
choices.B: Wait until all services recover before providing any stakeholder update
choices.C: Use only the failed email service so all communications remain in one system
choices.D: Create and exercise a crisis communication plan with authorized roles, stakeholder contacts, alternate channels, approval paths, and message validation

questions.explanation: A crisis communication plan should define audiences, authorized communicators, approval paths, alternate methods, and validation so messages remain timely and consistent when normal channels fail. Uncoordinated estimates can cause harm, silence may breach obligations and trust, and relying solely on an unavailable channel is not resilient.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Classifying information by the full impact of disclosure
questions.performanceIndicator: Evaluate confidentiality impact beyond financial loss or record type
questions.scenarioContext: An international relief organization maintains a small directory containing the current locations of temporary shelters for people escaping violence. The directory has little commercial value, but unauthorized disclosure could expose residents to physical harm.
questions.prompt: Which factor should have the GREATEST influence on the directory's classification?

choices.A: The small number of records in the directory
choices.B: The potential harm to individuals if the locations are disclosed
choices.C: The limited cost of recreating the directory
choices.D: The absence of proprietary financial information

questions.explanation: Classification should reflect the potential impact of compromise, including harm to people. Low volume, low recreation cost, and lack of commercial value do not reduce the severe confidentiality consequence created by exposing shelter locations. The sensitivity of an asset is not determined only by its size or monetary value.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Controlling secondary use by a data processor
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve controller authority over processing purposes when a processor proposes a new use
questions.scenarioContext: A payroll service provider processes employee data under a client's documented instructions. The provider asks to reuse the data to develop a separate workforce-benchmarking service that was not included in the original purpose.
questions.prompt: What should occur before the proposed use begins?

choices.A: The provider may proceed because it already possesses the data lawfully.
choices.B: The data custodian may approve the new purpose because it operates the storage platform.
choices.C: The controller must evaluate and explicitly authorize the new purpose and any resulting requirements.
choices.D: The provider may proceed after removing the client's classification labels.

questions.explanation: A processor acts on the controller's documented instructions and cannot independently create a materially different processing purpose. The controller must assess and authorize the new use, including necessary contractual and protection requirements. Possession, storage responsibility, or removal of labels does not establish authority for secondary use.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Handling media containing mixed classifications
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply protection based on the most restrictive information present when data cannot be segregated
questions.scenarioContext: A museum creates removable backup media containing public exhibit descriptions, internal operating procedures, and restricted donor records. The backup process does not separate the datasets onto different media.
questions.prompt: How should each backup medium be handled?

choices.A: According to the classification that represents the largest number of files
choices.B: As internal because the public and restricted content balance each other
choices.C: According to whichever dataset is restored most frequently
choices.D: At the most restrictive classification represented on the medium

questions.explanation: When information of different classifications is combined and cannot be separately controlled, the medium must receive protection sufficient for the most restrictive content. File volume and restoration frequency do not reduce the sensitivity of the donor records, and lower-classified data cannot offset higher-classified information.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Maintaining custody during physical transport
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply packaging, authorized transport, tracking, and receipt controls to classified assets
questions.scenarioContext: A film-production company must send restricted pre-release footage on encrypted media to a remote editing location. The recipient is authorized, but the standard courier service does not record custody transfers or verify the receiving individual.
questions.prompt: Which approach BEST meets the handling requirement?

choices.A: Use approved packaging and transport with documented custody, tracking, and verified receipt by an authorized person.
choices.B: Use the standard courier because encryption eliminates the need for physical accountability.
choices.C: Send two identical copies through different couriers to improve the chance of delivery.
choices.D: Remove the restricted marking so the package attracts less attention during transit.

questions.explanation: Classified physical assets require accountable transport in addition to technical safeguards. Approved packaging, documented custody transfers, tracking, and verified receipt preserve control throughout delivery. Encryption does not eliminate loss or custody requirements, duplicate shipments increase exposure, and removing a marking does not change the asset's classification.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Coordinating owner and custodian responsibilities
questions.performanceIndicator: Assign classification decisions to the data owner and implementation duties to the custodian
questions.scenarioContext: A renewable-energy company is introducing a new classification level for commercially sensitive site-acquisition records. The business executive designated as data owner and the infrastructure group acting as custodian must divide the work correctly.
questions.prompt: Which assignment of responsibilities is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: The custodian determines business sensitivity, and the owner operates the storage controls.
choices.B: The owner approves classification and authorized use, and the custodian implements the required controls.
choices.C: The owner configures every control, and the custodian approves new business purposes.
choices.D: The custodian approves classification and use whenever the infrastructure can support them.

questions.explanation: The data owner is accountable for classification and authorized use, while the custodian implements and operates the required technical and procedural safeguards. A custodian does not independently determine business sensitivity or authorize new purposes, and the owner provides requirements rather than personally administering every control.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Provisioning personally owned devices for business use
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply enrollment, minimum security, data separation, ownership, and exit requirements before a personal device accesses organizational assets
questions.scenarioContext: A real-estate brokerage permits agents to use personal tablets for client documents. Devices currently connect after only a password check, and the company has no inventory record, managed workspace, or process for removing business data when an agent leaves.
questions.prompt: What should be required BEFORE continued access is allowed?

choices.A: A signed statement that makes the agent solely responsible for any disclosure
choices.B: Annual confirmation that the tablet still belongs to the same agent
choices.C: Enrollment in an approved process enforcing minimum controls, business-data separation, inventory, and removal at exit
choices.D: A larger personal storage allowance so client documents do not need to be deleted

questions.explanation: Personally owned devices that handle organizational data still require controlled provisioning. Enrollment should establish an accountable inventory record, required safeguards, separation of business data, and an enforceable removal process. Liability statements and ownership checks do not implement protection, while additional storage encourages unnecessary retention.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Provisioning a software service as an organizational asset
questions.performanceIndicator: Establish ownership, approved use, data handling, inventory, support, and exit requirements before service adoption
questions.scenarioContext: A publishing company plans to adopt an online workflow service. The business sponsor has selected the service, but no one has documented the service owner, permitted information classifications, retention behavior, support responsibility, or export and deletion process at termination.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST next step?

choices.A: Complete the provisioning review and record lifecycle requirements before placing organizational data in the service.
choices.B: Begin with restricted data so the most demanding use case is tested immediately.
choices.C: Let each department decide independently which records the service may retain.
choices.D: Treat the service as a purchasing expense rather than an asset because the infrastructure is external.

questions.explanation: A hosted service must be provisioned as an organizational asset with accountable ownership and defined rules for classification, retention, support, export, and termination. Starting with restricted data creates exposure before requirements are established. Department-level improvisation is inconsistent, and external hosting does not remove lifecycle accountability.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Managing a pool of loaner equipment
questions.performanceIndicator: Maintain individual accountability and restore an approved state between temporary assignments
questions.scenarioContext: A hospital maintains loaner laptops for visiting clinicians. Devices are taken from an unlocked cabinet, users are not recorded, and returned laptops may still contain local files and customized settings from the previous borrower.
questions.prompt: Which TWO controls should be implemented? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Record each checkout and return against an identified user and asset.
choices.B: Allow borrowers to keep devices until another clinician specifically requests one.
choices.C: Restore and verify the approved baseline, including removal of prior-user data, before reassignment.
choices.D: Use a shared local account so every visiting clinician has the same experience.
choices.E: Remove inventory labels to discourage users from relying on a particular laptop.

questions.explanation: Checkout records establish custody and accountability, while restoring a verified baseline prevents one borrower's data and changes from carrying into the next assignment. Open-ended possession weakens inventory control, shared accounts reduce traceability, and removing labels makes asset reconciliation more difficult.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Applying retention based on message content
questions.performanceIndicator: Classify and retain business communications according to their function rather than their communication channel
questions.scenarioContext: A brokerage automatically deletes all collaboration messages after thirty days. Employees increasingly use the platform to approve transactions and document customer instructions that must be retained longer, while casual coordination messages have no continuing value.
questions.prompt: Which approach BEST addresses the retention problem?

choices.A: Retain every collaboration message indefinitely because some messages are records.
choices.B: Keep the thirty-day rule because retention should be based on the communication platform.
choices.C: Require employees to copy every message into email before it can become a record.
choices.D: Classify messages by business content and apply the appropriate record schedule regardless of channel.

questions.explanation: Record status and retention follow the business content and purpose, not the technology used to communicate. Content-based capture preserves transaction records while allowing transitory messages to expire. Indefinite retention creates unnecessary exposure, a channel-wide deletion period loses required records, and copying messages to email merely changes location.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Consolidating duplicate records without defeating retention controls
questions.performanceIndicator: Validate authoritative copies, holds, metadata, and required periods before disposing of duplicates
questions.scenarioContext: After a merger, a manufacturing group finds duplicate supplier records in two repositories. The repositories use different retention metadata, and one contains records associated with an active investigation. Management wants to delete one repository immediately to reduce cost.
questions.prompt: What should the records manager recommend?

choices.A: Delete the smaller repository because it is less likely to contain the authoritative copy.
choices.B: Reconcile content, ownership, metadata, and holds before designating authoritative copies and disposing of validated duplicates.
choices.C: Keep both repositories permanently because duplicate records cannot be safely consolidated.
choices.D: Export only the newest files and delete all older copies regardless of their scheduled retention.

questions.explanation: Consolidation should identify authoritative records and preserve required metadata, retention periods, and investigation holds before any copy is destroyed. Repository size or file age does not establish authority. Permanent duplication adds cost and exposure, while immediate deletion could remove required or held records.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Using a cloud access security broker for cloud data governance
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify cloud-service use and enforce classification-based policy across sanctioned and unsanctioned services
questions.scenarioContext: A design company discovers that employees upload project files to numerous cloud storage services. Security needs visibility into which services are used and a way to apply access and data-handling policy consistently across cloud activity.
questions.prompt: Which technology BEST addresses this requirement?

choices.A: Digital rights management limited to documents already selected for protection
choices.B: A records archive configured only for long-term preservation
choices.C: A cloud access security broker providing discovery, visibility, and policy enforcement
choices.D: A hardware asset inventory for company-issued endpoints

questions.explanation: A cloud access security broker is designed to provide visibility into cloud-service use and enforce organizational access and data policies across cloud interactions. Digital rights management protects designated content but does not discover the broader service landscape. Archiving and endpoint inventory address different lifecycle and asset-management needs.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Applying persistent usage controls with digital rights management
questions.performanceIndicator: Maintain document-use restrictions after authorized distribution
questions.scenarioContext: An investment firm distributes confidential research reports to approved external advisers. The firm needs to restrict forwarding and printing and to revoke access when an adviser's engagement ends, even after the report has been delivered.
questions.prompt: Which control is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Digital rights management that applies persistent usage restrictions and revocation to the reports
choices.B: A longer archive period for all copies sent to external advisers
choices.C: A cloud inventory that lists services but does not control delivered documents
choices.D: A data classification label without an enforcement mechanism

questions.explanation: Digital rights management can attach persistent controls to designated documents, including restrictions on use and the ability to revoke access after distribution. Retention does not constrain recipient actions, service inventory does not govern the delivered report, and a label communicates requirements but does not enforce them by itself.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Sanitizing data-bearing office equipment before return
questions.performanceIndicator: Account for embedded storage and verify sanitization when leased equipment leaves organizational custody
questions.scenarioContext: A government contractor is returning leased multifunction printers. The devices scanned restricted documents and contain internal storage, but the facilities team treats them as ordinary office furniture and plans to release them directly to the lessor.
questions.prompt: What should the security manager require before release?

choices.A: Delete stored address-book entries because document images expire automatically.
choices.B: Obtain a confidentiality promise from the delivery driver.
choices.C: Remove the asset tags because ownership is returning to the lessor.
choices.D: Identify the embedded media and perform or verify approved sanitization appropriate to the data and disposition.

questions.explanation: Multifunction devices can retain document data on embedded storage and must be handled as data-bearing assets. Approved, verified sanitization should occur before the equipment leaves custody. Address-book deletion is incomplete, a driver's promise does not remove remanence, and asset-tag removal is administrative rather than protective.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Protecting sensitive data during active troubleshooting
questions.performanceIndicator: Limit exposure and residual copies when sensitive data is in use for diagnostic activity
questions.scenarioContext: Engineers troubleshoot a production billing service by capturing memory dumps that may contain customer data in use. The dumps are copied to a broad team workspace and remain there after incidents close.
questions.prompt: Which TWO controls most directly reduce this exposure? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Retain every dump indefinitely in case a similar defect appears later.
choices.B: Restrict diagnostic captures to authorized personnel and approved protected locations.
choices.C: Treat the dumps as nonsensitive because they were created for troubleshooting.
choices.D: Permit engineers to move dumps to personal storage when the shared workspace is full.
choices.E: Apply a defined retention period and securely dispose of dumps when the diagnostic need ends.

questions.explanation: Memory dumps can contain sensitive data in use, so access and storage locations should be tightly controlled and copies removed when the approved diagnostic need ends. Their technical purpose does not lower sensitivity. Indefinite or personal retention expands exposure and defeats accountable lifecycle management.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Verifying destruction of versioned cloud data
questions.performanceIndicator: Ensure approved deletion reaches active objects, retained versions, replicas, and recoverable copies within the provider's scope
questions.scenarioContext: A travel company approves destruction of an expired customer dataset stored in a versioned cloud repository. An administrator deletes the current objects, but earlier versions and replicated copies remain recoverable under the service's standard settings.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST completion criterion for the destruction process?

choices.A: The current objects no longer appear in the ordinary user interface.
choices.B: The administrator records that a delete command was issued successfully.
choices.C: All in-scope versions and replicas are removed or expire under an approved, verified destruction process.
choices.D: The data owner can no longer open the original object links.

questions.explanation: Destruction is complete only when all copies within the approved scope, including recoverable versions and replicas, are addressed and the result is verified. Hiding current objects, logging a command, or breaking links may leave the underlying information recoverable and therefore still retained.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Applying the Brewer-Nash model to conflicts of interest
questions.performanceIndicator: Select a dynamic information-flow model that isolates competing client datasets
questions.scenarioContext: A consulting firm serves several direct competitors. Once a consultant accesses confidential information for one client, the platform must prevent that consultant from accessing confidential information belonging to competing clients while still allowing access to public industry data.
questions.prompt: Which formal security model MOST directly supports this requirement?

choices.A: Brewer-Nash
choices.B: Bell-LaPadula
choices.C: Biba
choices.D: Clark-Wilson

questions.explanation: Brewer-Nash, also called the Chinese Wall model, dynamically restricts access based on information previously accessed to prevent conflicts of interest. Bell-LaPadula emphasizes confidentiality labels, Biba emphasizes integrity levels, and Clark-Wilson protects commercial integrity through constrained transactions and separation of duties.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Preserving secure state transitions
questions.performanceIndicator: Ensure every transition maintains defined security invariants
questions.scenarioContext: A secure workflow begins in an approved state, but an error-recovery path can move a transaction directly from pending review to completed without evaluating mandatory authorization rules.
questions.prompt: From a state-machine security perspective, what is the PRIMARY design defect?

choices.A: The workflow contains more than one operational state.
choices.B: The recovery path records a different timestamp than the normal path.
choices.C: A permitted transition can move the system into a state that violates a security invariant.
choices.D: The completed state cannot return automatically to the pending state.

questions.explanation: A secure state-machine design requires every allowed transition to preserve the system's defined security properties. Bypassing mandatory authorization creates an insecure reachable state. Multiple states and different timestamps are not inherently defects, and inability to reverse a completed transaction does not explain the authorization failure.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Applying least privilege to automated service identities
questions.performanceIndicator: Limit a service to the specific resources and operations its function requires
questions.scenarioContext: A report-generation service reads approved records from one database view and writes finished reports to one storage location. It currently runs using an infrastructure administrator identity with broad access across the environment.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST implements least privilege?

choices.A: Retain the administrator identity but rotate its password more frequently.
choices.B: Use the administrator identity only during business hours and disable it overnight.
choices.C: Share the administrator identity with a backup service to improve availability.
choices.D: Assign a dedicated identity limited to the required database read and report-storage write operations.

questions.explanation: A dedicated identity with narrowly scoped permissions limits both routine authority and the impact of service compromise. Password rotation does not reduce authorization scope. Time restrictions leave excessive privileges during operation, and sharing the identity increases exposure and weakens accountability.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Designing independent layers of protection
questions.performanceIndicator: Select complementary controls that continue limiting impact after one layer fails
questions.scenarioContext: A public benefits application relies on one application gateway to block malicious requests. If the gateway is bypassed, the backend accepts any syntactically valid request and the database identity can modify every application table.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST applies defense in depth?

choices.A: Add a second identical gateway rule set but leave backend authorization and database privileges unchanged.
choices.B: Retain the gateway while adding backend authorization, strict input handling, narrowly scoped database access, and monitoring at each boundary.
choices.C: Increase gateway logging capacity and continue trusting all requests that reach the backend.
choices.D: Hide the backend address from documentation and preserve the existing database identity.

questions.explanation: Complementary enforcement at the gateway, application, database, and monitoring layers prevents one failed or bypassed control from exposing the entire system. A duplicate rule set may repeat the same weakness. More gateway logging remains dependent on one enforcement point, and hiding an address is not a reliable security boundary.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Applying trust-but-verify to a managed platform
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify independent assurance mechanisms for externally operated controls
questions.scenarioContext: A company uses a managed analytics platform whose operator is responsible for infrastructure hardening and backup execution. The company remains accountable for protecting its information and cannot rely only on the operator's verbal assurances.
questions.prompt: Which TWO actions BEST implement trust but verify? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Assume that advertised platform features are enabled for every tenant configuration.
choices.B: Transfer all risk ownership to the operator because the infrastructure is managed externally.
choices.C: Define control responsibilities and obtain appropriate evidence that the operator performs its assigned controls.
choices.D: Disable customer-side logging so the operator remains the only source of security information.
choices.E: Independently monitor customer-visible configurations, access, backup results, and exceptions against requirements.

questions.explanation: Clear responsibility mapping establishes what must be verified, while independent monitoring and suitable evidence test whether controls operate as expected. Feature claims do not prove tenant configuration. Accountability cannot be transferred entirely, and disabling customer visibility removes an important verification capability.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Preventing backend access from bypassing protective gateways
questions.performanceIndicator: Ensure server components accept traffic only through authorized architectural paths
questions.scenarioContext: An online reservation service routes public traffic through a protective application gateway, but the backend servers also have public addresses and accept direct requests that never pass through the gateway.
questions.prompt: Which architectural correction MOST directly closes the bypass?

choices.A: Increase the gateway's processing capacity while leaving the backend publicly reachable.
choices.B: Remove direct public reachability and allow backend requests only from authorized gateway paths with authenticated service communication.
choices.C: Add a banner to the backend stating that direct connections are prohibited.
choices.D: Retain public backend access but use less descriptive server hostnames.

questions.explanation: Restricting backend reachability to authenticated gateway paths makes the intended control boundary enforceable. More gateway capacity does not affect direct access. A warning banner is administrative, and obscure hostnames do not prevent discovery or connection.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Separating database encryption keys from encrypted data
questions.performanceIndicator: Reduce common-mode compromise in database encryption architecture
questions.scenarioContext: A database server encrypts data files, but the only copy of the master encryption key is stored in a readable configuration file on the same server under the same administrative control.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST reduces the common-mode exposure?

choices.A: Rename the key file and move it to another directory on the same server.
choices.B: Compress the encrypted data files before placing them on storage media.
choices.C: Use a longer configuration-file name and restrict access to database users only.
choices.D: Protect the master key in a separate controlled key-management boundary and authorize database use without exposing raw key material.

questions.explanation: A separate controlled key-management boundary prevents compromise of the database host from automatically yielding both ciphertext and the master key. Renaming or relocating the file on the same host preserves the shared failure domain. Compression and filename length do not protect keys.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Designing secure onboarding for Internet of Things devices
questions.performanceIndicator: Replace shared factory credentials with unique authenticated enrollment
questions.scenarioContext: A property-management company is deploying thousands of smart meters. Every meter arrives with the same factory administrator password, and installers plan to leave that credential active after connecting devices to the management platform.
questions.prompt: Which onboarding architecture is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Give each device a unique identity, authenticate enrollment, replace or disable factory credentials, and bind the device to its authorized owner.
choices.B: Keep the shared credential but change the management portal's display name after deployment.
choices.C: Publish the factory password only to installers and assume it will remain confidential.
choices.D: Place meters in multiple buildings while retaining the same credential to simplify support.

questions.explanation: Unique device identity, authenticated enrollment, removal of shared defaults, and ownership binding prevent compromise of one credential from exposing the full fleet. A portal name has no authentication value. Limiting initial distribution cannot make a fleet-wide shared secret safe, and physical distribution across buildings does not reduce credential reuse risk.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Preventing duplicate execution in distributed transactions
questions.performanceIndicator: Design idempotent processing and replay detection for retried messages
questions.scenarioContext: A distributed payment workflow retries messages when acknowledgments are delayed. An attacker can replay a previously valid request, and the receiving service currently creates a new transfer each time the message arrives.
questions.prompt: Which architectural control BEST addresses this risk?

choices.A: Increase the message retry interval while allowing every received request to create a transfer.
choices.B: Encrypt the message queue but do not track previously processed requests.
choices.C: Authenticate requests and enforce idempotent processing using unique transaction identifiers, freshness checks, and recorded completion state.
choices.D: Add more receiving-service instances and distribute replayed requests among them.

questions.explanation: Authenticated requests combined with unique identifiers, freshness validation, and durable completion state allow safe retries while rejecting or neutralizing replays. Longer intervals do not prevent duplicates. Queue encryption protects confidentiality but not repeated valid messages, and additional instances can increase concurrency without establishing transaction uniqueness.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Reducing attack surface in event-driven serverless systems
questions.performanceIndicator: Constrain function identities and event sources to intended operations
questions.scenarioContext: An event-driven document service uses many short-lived functions. Every function shares one broad execution role, and any account in the environment can create events that invoke sensitive processing functions.
questions.prompt: Which TWO changes BEST reduce the architectural exposure? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Increase function memory allocation while retaining the shared execution role.
choices.B: Assign each function a narrowly scoped execution identity based on its required resources and actions.
choices.C: Store additional event copies so failed processing can be retried more often.
choices.D: Restrict and authenticate permitted event sources before sensitive functions can be invoked.
choices.E: Use a longer common role name so accidental selection becomes less likely.

questions.explanation: Function-specific least privilege limits the effect of compromise, while authenticated and restricted triggers prevent unauthorized invocation. Memory size and event-copy count concern capacity or reliability rather than authorization. A longer role name does not reduce the role's excessive permissions.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Validating certificate chains and intended identities
questions.performanceIndicator: Verify trust path, validity, revocation, usage, and subject identity
questions.scenarioContext: An application accepts any certificate signed by a trusted root. It does not verify the requested service identity or whether the certificate is authorized for the intended purpose.
questions.prompt: What validation should the architect require?

choices.A: Verify only that the certificate contains a public key of the expected length.
choices.B: Accept the certificate when its subject field contains any organization name.
choices.C: Validate the trust chain, validity and revocation status, permitted key usage, and the certificate identity expected for the service.
choices.D: Store a local copy of the certificate without evaluating its identity or purpose.

questions.explanation: A valid signature chain alone does not prove that a certificate represents the intended service or is authorized for the requested use. Complete validation includes chain construction, time validity, revocation status, key-usage constraints, and expected identity. Key length, a generic organization name, or local storage cannot substitute for those checks.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Limiting cryptographic compromise through key hierarchy
questions.performanceIndicator: Use separate data keys and controlled wrapping keys to reduce blast radius
questions.scenarioContext: A multi-tenant archive encrypts every customer's files directly with one long-lived symmetric key. Management wants to rotate protection without re-encrypting all file contents and to limit the impact of one tenant-key compromise.
questions.prompt: Which design BEST meets these goals?

choices.A: Use separate data-encryption keys by appropriate scope and wrap them with controlled key-encryption keys that can be rotated independently.
choices.B: Keep one long-lived content key but rename it for each tenant in application metadata.
choices.C: Hash the common encryption key and publish the hash with every archived file.
choices.D: Duplicate the common key across additional servers so it remains available during maintenance.

questions.explanation: Scoped data-encryption keys reduce compromise impact, while wrapping them with separately managed key-encryption keys supports efficient rotation by rewrapping keys rather than re-encrypting all content. Renaming does not create distinct keys. Publishing a hash adds no protection, and copying the same key expands its exposure.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Selecting a keyed integrity mechanism
questions.performanceIndicator: Distinguish message authentication codes from unkeyed hashes
questions.scenarioContext: Two internal systems already share a protected symmetric secret. The receiving system must detect message modification and verify that a party holding the shared secret generated the message. Confidentiality is not required.
questions.prompt: Which mechanism is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: A plain checksum transmitted with the message
choices.B: An unkeyed cryptographic hash stored beside the message
choices.C: Reversible encoding using a format known only to the two systems
choices.D: A hash-based message authentication code computed with the shared secret

questions.explanation: A hash-based message authentication code uses the shared secret to provide integrity and symmetric origin authentication. A checksum or unkeyed hash can be recomputed by an attacker who changes the message. Reversible encoding is not a cryptographic integrity control.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Recognizing a ciphertext-only attack condition
questions.performanceIndicator: Classify cryptanalysis when only encrypted messages are available
questions.prompt: An attacker possesses a collection of encrypted messages but has no corresponding plaintext, encryption key, or ability to request chosen encryptions or decryptions. Which attack condition is described?

choices.A: Known-plaintext
choices.B: Ciphertext-only
choices.C: Chosen-plaintext
choices.D: Side-channel

questions.explanation: A ciphertext-only attack begins with encrypted messages and no matching plaintext or oracle access. Known-plaintext includes some matching plaintext and ciphertext. Chosen-plaintext involves obtaining encryptions of selected inputs, while side-channel attacks exploit implementation leakage such as timing or power use.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Protecting cryptographic key generation from weak entropy
questions.performanceIndicator: Select an approved unpredictable random source and detect generator failure
questions.scenarioContext: An embedded controller generates encryption keys immediately after startup using only its current clock value. Devices powered on together frequently create identical keys.
questions.prompt: Which correction BEST addresses the cryptographic weakness?

choices.A: Use an approved cryptographically secure random generator seeded with sufficient unpredictable entropy and monitor for generator failure.
choices.B: Format the clock value in a longer text string before using it as the key.
choices.C: Generate keys at the same scheduled time so administrators can reproduce them if needed.
choices.D: Encode duplicate keys before storing them on each controller.

questions.explanation: Cryptographic keys require sufficient unpredictable entropy from an approved generator; health checks help identify a failed random source. A longer representation does not add entropy. Scheduled generation increases predictability, and encoding identical keys does not make them independent or random.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Using environmental design to improve perimeter visibility
questions.performanceIndicator: Select landscaping and boundary features that support natural surveillance and controlled access
questions.scenarioContext: A small data-processing site has dense shrubs beside ground-floor windows and tall landscaping that conceals portions of the pedestrian approach from guards and cameras.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST applies security-conscious environmental design?

choices.A: Add taller opaque vegetation along the entire building to discourage observation from outside.
choices.B: Move cameras indoors and retain the concealed exterior approach.
choices.C: Create additional informal paths through the landscaping so pedestrians can choose their own route.
choices.D: Use low or appropriately spaced landscaping, preserve clear sight lines, and channel visitors toward monitored entrances.

questions.explanation: Clear sight lines and defined movement toward monitored entrances increase natural surveillance and reduce concealment. Taller opaque vegetation creates hiding places. Indoor-only cameras do not restore exterior visibility, and informal paths weaken controlled access and make observation more difficult.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Controlling electrostatic discharge in equipment areas
questions.performanceIndicator: Combine grounding, environmental control, and handling procedures to protect components
questions.scenarioContext: A hardware repair room experiences unexplained component failures during dry weather. Technicians work on synthetic carpet, humidity falls below the approved range, and no grounded work surfaces or wrist straps are provided.
questions.prompt: Which corrective design is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Increase room temperature and continue using the existing carpet and work surfaces.
choices.B: Store components in ordinary plastic bags and require technicians to touch a wall before repairs.
choices.C: Install grounded static-dissipative surfaces, use appropriate personal grounding and packaging, and maintain humidity within the approved range.
choices.D: Disable environmental alarms during dry weather to reduce unnecessary work interruptions.

questions.explanation: Static-dissipative grounded surfaces, personal grounding, protective packaging, and controlled humidity address the generation and discharge of static electricity. Temperature alone does not solve the problem. Ordinary plastic can generate static, touching a wall is unreliable, and disabling alarms conceals rather than reduces risk.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Protecting utility and communications service entrances
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify controls that reduce single-path disruption and unauthorized demarcation access
questions.scenarioContext: A financial processing facility receives both primary communications circuits through one exposed conduit and places the carrier demarcation panels in an unlocked shared maintenance closet.
questions.prompt: Which TWO changes BEST reduce the identified risks? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Use physically diverse service routes where justified so one local event is less likely to sever every circuit.
choices.B: Label the shared conduit more clearly while retaining both circuits in the same exposed path.
choices.C: Move the demarcation panels into the public lobby so carrier technicians can reach them easily.
choices.D: Terminate both circuits on one unprotected panel to simplify maintenance.
choices.E: Place demarcation equipment in a restricted, monitored area with controlled maintenance access.

questions.explanation: Physically diverse routes reduce common-path failure, while restricted and monitored demarcation space prevents casual tampering and records authorized access. Labels do not create route diversity. Public placement increases exposure, and a single unprotected panel preserves a common failure and attack point.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Balancing emergency egress with access control
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve life safety while detecting and limiting misuse of emergency exits
questions.scenarioContext: A museum's emergency exits allow immediate evacuation as required, but intruders have used the same doors to enter a restricted archive when staff temporarily defeated the door contacts to stop nuisance alarms.
questions.prompt: Which design is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Lock the emergency exits from both directions until a security officer approves each evacuation.
choices.B: Preserve code-compliant free egress while using monitored door hardware, reliable alarms, exterior-entry protection, and a defined response process.
choices.C: Disable all exit alarms during public hours and rely on staff observation.
choices.D: Replace emergency exits with access-controlled revolving doors.

questions.explanation: Life safety requires code-compliant egress, while monitored hardware, protected exterior entry, dependable alarms, and response procedures address unauthorized use. Locking evacuation routes or using unsuitable barriers can endanger occupants. Disabling alarms removes detection rather than correcting nuisance-alarm causes.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Controlling temporary facility-security bypasses during maintenance
questions.performanceIndicator: Authorize, monitor, expire, and verify removal of compensating arrangements
questions.scenarioContext: During a two-week renovation, contractors need equipment access through a normally alarmed service door. Previous projects left temporary access badges and alarm bypasses active after work ended.
questions.prompt: Which approach BEST protects the facility throughout the maintenance period?

choices.A: Disable the service-door alarm for the entire project and depend on contractors to report unusual activity.
choices.B: Issue permanent badges to the contractor supervisor so future projects require less setup.
choices.C: Use approved time-limited access and documented bypasses, add compensating monitoring, and verify restoration and credential revocation at closeout.
choices.D: Leave the normal alarm enabled but provide all contractors with the shared employee door code.

questions.explanation: Time-limited authorization, documented exceptions, compensating monitoring, and formal closeout control the temporary need and ensure normal protection is restored. A project-long unmonitored bypass creates exposure. Permanent or shared credentials outlive the work and weaken accountability.

questions.competency: IV.A — Network Architecture Fundamentals
questions.skill: Mitigating local address resolution spoofing
questions.performanceIndicator: Select access-layer validation that protects IP-to-MAC address resolution
questions.scenarioContext: A corporate office experiences intermittent interception of traffic within one IPv4 subnet. Investigation shows that a malicious workstation is sending forged address resolution messages so other hosts associate the default gateway address with the attacker's network interface.
questions.prompt: Which control would MOST directly mitigate this attack?

choices.A: Increase the external firewall's idle session timeout.
choices.B: Change the public DNS record for the default gateway.
choices.C: Use trusted address-binding information to validate address resolution messages on access switches.
choices.D: Enable route summarization on the Internet edge router.

questions.explanation: Access-switch validation based on trusted IP-to-MAC bindings can reject forged address resolution messages on the local segment. External firewall timers, public DNS, and route summarization operate outside the local resolution process and do not stop the spoofing behavior.

questions.competency: IV.A — Network Architecture Fundamentals
questions.skill: Maintaining DNS policy when queries are encrypted
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve approved name resolution and monitoring paths for managed endpoints
